HTML Editor for Email

Manual

An editor for the body of an HTML email. No signup, no login. What you write stays in your browser and is never sent anywhere.

01What this is

This editor produces the HTML that becomes the body of an email. It does not send mail. You take the finished body and paste it into whatever mail client you already use.

HTML for email is not HTML for the web. Mail clients strip and ignore much of what a browser accepts, so the output here is built for those constraints from the start:

  • Layout is built from tables, not modern CSS layout
  • Every bit of styling is written directly on the tag
  • The body is 600px wide
  • Every image carries alt text

Those four are the floor for rendering correctly across mail clients. Every template and every part follows them.

Everything is stored in this browser. There is no server. You can confirm nothing leaves your machine by opening your browser's developer tools and watching the network tab. The trade-off is that your work is not visible on another device or another browser.

02The screen

Three areas:

AreaWhat it does
Left Your documents, split into Drafts and Archive
Middle Where you edit — preview, code, or both side by side
Right Settings for whatever you have selected: size, colour, spacing

Three ways to work

Switch with Preview / Code / Preview + code at the top.

  • Preview — edit the text directly on the finished layout. This is enough most of the time
  • Code — edit the HTML itself
  • Preview + code — both at once; a change on either side shows up on the other

Making room

Both side panels collapse. On a short screen, set Interface size to Small to fit more on screen at once. This does not change how the email looks — only the app around it.

03Your first email

  1. Pick a template

    Press Start from a template. There are 34, in six groups. Pick the one closest to what you are writing.

  2. Choose the look

    Look and Accent sit above the list. Decide the look first — every thumbnail updates as you click, so you are choosing from 34 designs you already like.

  3. Write your text

    Click any text in the preview and type over it. Headings, body copy, button labels — all the same gesture.

  4. Add your signature

    Sender details go at the end. Save one and it is one click from then on.

  5. Save

    Save or Ctrl + S. It appears under Drafts on the left.

  6. Get it into email

    Send as email, then Copy the body, then Open Gmail or Open Outlook, and paste. Details below.

04Templates and looks

There are 34 templates in six groups.

GroupWhat's in it
BasicsAnnouncement, plain, empty
AnnouncementsCall to action, header image, event invitation, newsletter, and more
TransactionalOrder confirmation, shipping notice, password reset
RequestsSending a document, arranging a time, asking for a survey response
InternalTeam notices, meeting notes, action requests
Web pageFor pages, not email

Five genres, not five palettes

Changing the genre changes the construction, not just the colour. Heading treatment, button shape and width, line height, density, rules, typeface, columns, and even the order of the sections all move.

GenreSuitsAccents
BusinessEveryday correspondence with clients and partnersBlue, navy, green, grey
FormalInvitations, ceremonies, anything that needs weightNavy, forest, wine, ink
CasualPeople you know, internal notes, light announcementsOrange, teal, rose, violet
PopCampaigns, sign-ups, anything that needs to catch the eyeRose, orange, blue, green, purple
MinimalNotices and admin mail that should not look decoratedBlack, grey

34 templates across 19 look-and-accent combinations comes to 646 finished designs. The list is deliberately not 646 items long — scrolling 646 cards is harder, not easier. Set the look first, then choose from 34.

Saving your own

Once a layout is one you keep reaching for, open it and press Save the current document in the template dialog. It appears at the top of the list from then on. Saving under an existing name replaces it.

05Editing

On the preview

Click text and type. Select a range and a small toolbar appears with bold, italic, underline, lists and headings.

Click the edge of a block to select the block itself. The right panel then shows its settings, and Move up / Move down reorder it.

The font list is short on purpose. It contains only faces that survive in email. A font the recipient does not have is silently swapped for one they do, so offering more would only produce surprises.

Adding parts

Ten parts can be dropped in: Heading, Body, Button, Image, Info table, Callout box, Divider, Spacing, Two columns, Signature.

Each can go Insert at the selection or at the end of the body.

Images

You cannot attach an image file. Point to a URL instead.

None of the ways of embedding an image work in email any more. Data URIs are stripped by Gmail, and direct links from cloud storage were closed off. Hosting the image somewhere and linking to it is the only reliable route left.

Many people read mail with images turned off, so always write the alt text. It is what they will see instead.

In code

Switch to Code to edit the HTML directly, or Preview + code to watch the result as you type.

Canvas width at the top lets you try widths other than 600px. 600px is the de facto standard, though — go wider and some clients will make the reader scroll sideways.

06How saving works

Documents live in Drafts or Archive. The idea is that work in progress sits in Drafts and finished work moves to Archive. Neither has a limit on how many you keep.

Every save keeps a version

Each save records the document as it was. Select a document and press Restore this version to go back to any of them. This exists for the moment an AI rewrite turns out worse than what you had.

When your work disappears

Storage is your browser's own (localStorage). Documents are lost if:

  • you clear your browsing data (cookies and site data)
  • you work in a private or incognito window and close it
  • you open the editor on another device or in another browser — it was never there

For anything you need to keep, use Save as a file or Export as a web page and put it somewhere you control.

Storage has a size limit too. As it fills, the oldest versions are dropped automatically. The documents themselves are never dropped.

07Signatures

Save the signatures you use and inserting one at the end of the body becomes a single click. These are stored in your browser as well.

The default shape is four lines:

  1. Company and team
  2. Name
  3. Postal address
  4. Contact

Keep the address line. If you are sending anything promotional, several jurisdictions require a physical postal address in the message itself — the US CAN-SPAM Act among them. The address line is there so you do not have to remember.

08Ask AI

The editor is not connected to any AI. What it does is assemble the request for you. You copy that out and paste it into whichever assistant you use — nothing here is tied to one service.

  1. Choose the kind of request

    Nine of them: draft the wording, polish the wording, make it more formal, make it shorter, improve the look, add some styling, fix the HTML, make it readable on a phone, translate to English.

  2. Add anything specific

    "Rewrite for a younger audience", for instance. You can leave it empty.

  3. Copy the prompt

    Copy the prompt. You choose whether the current document is included.

  4. Paste the answer back

    Put the HTML that comes back into Replace everything. If you do not like it, go back to a saved version.

Requests you make often can be kept with Save this request; they then appear alongside the nine built-in ones.

Save before you replace. A saved document can be brought back with Restore this version if the rewrite is not what you wanted.

09Getting it into email

Send as email at the top offers four routes.

Gmail and Outlook

Copy, then paste. Neither Gmail nor Outlook on the web can import a prepared message file, so pasting is the only way in.

  1. Press Copy the body

    The formatting comes with it.

  2. Press Open Gmail or Open Outlook

    A new tab opens on a blank draft.

  3. Paste into the body field

    Ctrl + V. Fill in the subject and recipients there as usual.

Copying and opening are separate buttons because the order matters. Once you have switched tabs, going back to copy is awkward. Copy first, then open.

A desktop mail client

Save as a file writes a message file (.eml). If your desktop mail client is associated with that type, opening it gives you a draft. Support varies between clients.

As a web page

Export as a web page writes a standalone HTML file you can open in a browser — useful when the piece is going on an intranet or a notice page rather than into an inbox.

10Keyboard

KeysDoes
Ctrl + SSave
Ctrl + ZUndo
Ctrl + DDuplicate the selected block
DeleteRemove the selected block (does nothing while editing text)
EscDrop the selection, stop editing, close a dialog

On a Mac, ⌘ instead of Ctrl.

11If something goes wrong

The paste arrived as plain text

Check that nothing else was copied in between, and that you pasted into the body field rather than the subject line.

A document is missing

Make sure you are in the same browser and the same profile. Documents are not shared with another device, another browser, or a private window. See how saving works.

It renders badly for the recipient

Check that the body is not wider than 600px and that the template's table structure is intact. Some clients cannot render deeply nested layouts. Asking an AI to make it readable on a phone is often the quickest fix.

The interface is in the wrong language

The editor opens in your browser's language. To change it, use the language list at the top right. English and Japanese are available for now.
